reason: Research this week supports the floating-rate carry thesis. The Fed hiked 25bp in September 2026 to 3.75-4.00% and held on Oct 28 with two dissents (Cook, Hammack) who wanted another hike. A hot October CPI (~Nov 10) pushed CME FedWatch December-hike odds to about 85%, with a growing tail on 50bp (Waller argued for 50bp; Kalshi showed about 97% for any hike). The 66% in AAA CLO floaters (JAAA 50, ICLO 16) resets roughly 25-50bp higher within a quarter of a December move, while the engine's cash stays fixed at 4%, so these yields (about SOFR + ~120bp, or 5%+) keep pulling further ahead of cash. AAA spreads were last seen range-bound around 116-122bp (September new issue and refis; I found no November data). I found no sign of AAA credit stress. Weakness has been confined to the BB/B tranches, which this book does not own. AMLP (16%, fee-based midstream) stays as the energy and inflation hedge in a hot-CPI regime. SPYI (8%) is small, and covered-call income partly cushions a hawkish equity wobble. The current leg is near flat (JAAA +0.61%, ICLO +0.52%, AMLP -0.23%, SPYI -0.35%). The lifetime -2.38% comes from earlier legs, not this book. The alternatives are marginal. Moving the 10% cash into JAAA adds only about 1-1.5% a year on 10% of capital, roughly 10-15bp of book NAV a year, and I want the buffer kept against a 50bp-surprise risk-off. Swapping SPYI for a Treasury floater (USFR) gains a few bp at best. Neither justifies churn, so holding beats trading. Limits: I could not find November 2026 CLO spread data, current JAAA yield or the 11-13 week's equity and oil tape, so the credit-spread and AMLP views rest partly on September data and the packet marks.
